text: This course assumes you already know Python's basics, but quantum simulation code has a specific habit of turning into an unreadable pile of matrix literals if you don't organize it deliberately. This lesson reviews functions and classes through exactly that lens, using a small Qubit class as the running example.

A function should take what it needs as arguments and return what it computes, not silently depend on variables sitting outside it. A class is how Python bundles state and behavior together, so a qubit's amplitudes and the operations that make sense on them travel as one object instead of loose numbers passed between functions. And a method that only reads state, like computing a probability, is a very different thing from one that changes it, like applying a gate.

Here's a Qubit class with its state set once in __init__, and a probabilities method that reads self dot alpha and self dot beta and returns P of zero and P of one without ever modifying the qubit. For alpha 0.6 and beta 0.8, that comes out to 0.36 and 0.64, a genuine unequal split between outcomes.

apply_gate deliberately returns a brand-new Qubit instead of overwriting self dot alpha and self dot beta in place. That keeps every intermediate state inspectable as a simulation chains several gates together. And defining __repr__ once means printing q shows you the actual amplitudes, Qubit alpha equals 0.6000, beta equals 0.8000, instead of Python's default, nearly useless memory-address output.
Next lesson moves into Jupyter notebooks, the interactive tool you'll use to run and modify almost every NumPy and plotting example for the rest of this course.
